title: Fake CAPTCHA Attacks Are Exploding: How ClickFix Became the Web's Most Dangerous Social Engineering Trick
excerpt: Cybersecurity researchers warn that fake CAPTCHA pages now account for nearly half of all initial access attacks, tricking users into running malware on their own machines.
body:
• ClickFix-style fake CAPTCHA attacks now account for 47% of initial access methods observed by Microsoft, with over 147,000 systems infected since late 2025
  • The attacks trick users into pasting malicious PowerShell commands into Windows Run dialogs, bypassing antivirus and endpoint detection tools entirely
  • New variants including ErrTraffic, ClearFake, and state-sponsored campaigns by Russia's GRU are expanding the threat across compromised WordPress sites, enterprise environments, and government targets
  • The malware delivered includes info-stealers targeting browser credentials, cryptocurrency wallets, and email accounts

Cybersecurity researchers are sounding alarms about a rapidly growing class of attacks that weaponize one of the internet's most familiar security features: the CAPTCHA verification page. Known as ClickFix, the technique uses fake CAPTCHA challenges to trick users into executing malicious commands on their own computers — and it has become the single most common initial access method observed in the wild.

According to Microsoft's latest threat intelligence, ClickFix-style attacks accounted for 47% of all observed initial access incidents. Analysis by security firm Expel estimates that over 147,521 systems have been infected through the ClearFake campaign alone since late August 2025.

How the Attack Works

The mechanics are deceptively simple. A user visits a compromised website — often a legitimate WordPress site that has been injected with malicious JavaScript. Instead of showing normal content, the page displays what appears to be a Cloudflare Turnstile verification or Google reCAPTCHA challenge.

Rather than asking users to identify traffic lights or crosswalks, the fake CAPTCHA instructs them to press Windows Key + R to open the Run dialog, then Ctrl + V to paste a command, then Enter to execute it. What the user doesn't realize is that malicious PowerShell code has already been silently copied to their clipboard by the page's JavaScript.

"Defending against the ClickFix technique is uniquely challenging because the attack chain is built almost entirely on legitimate user actions and the abuse of trusted system tools."

— Martin Zugec, Technical Solutions Director, Bitdefender

Because the user executes the command themselves using built-in Windows tools, antivirus software and endpoint detection systems treat it as a trusted action. The malware runs in memory, injects itself into legitimate system processes like svchost.exe, and begins exfiltrating data without writing files to disk.

An Evolving Threat Ecosystem

The ClickFix landscape has grown far beyond its origins. Researchers have identified multiple variants including FileFix, JackFix, CrashFix, and GlitchFix, each using different social engineering pretexts to convince users to execute commands.

The latest entrant, ErrTraffic, is a traffic distribution system specifically designed for ClickFix campaigns. It actively corrupts the visual appearance of compromised web pages using CSS transformations, making them look broken, then suggests a "fix" that triggers malware execution. "ErrTraffic doesn't just show a fake update prompt, it actively corrupts the underlying page to make victims believe something is genuinely wrong," according to researchers at Censys.

Meanwhile, the ClearFake framework has infected at least 9,300 WordPress sites and uses blockchain smart contracts on Binance's BNB Smart Chain to store attack infrastructure, making traditional takedowns ineffective. The attack chain deploys info-stealers including Lumma Stealer, Vidar Stealer, and StealC, which harvest browser credentials, cryptocurrency wallet data, email logins, and system information.

State-Sponsored Adoption

The technique has also been adopted by nation-state actors. In July 2026, Ukraine's Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-UA) attributed a fake CAPTCHA campaign to UAC-0145, a sub-cluster of Sandworm — the advanced hacking unit affiliated with Russia's GRU military intelligence agency. That campaign deployed multiple malware families including GHETTOVIBE for persistence, SCOUTCURL for reconnaissance, and FREAKYPOLL for persistent remote access, according to The Hacker News.

The GRU campaign stored command-and-control server addresses inside Ethereum smart contracts — immutable blockchain code that cannot be seized, deleted, or taken offline by law enforcement.

How to Protect Yourself

Security researchers stress that no legitimate website will ever ask users to open the Windows Run dialog or paste commands into a terminal as part of a verification process. Any CAPTCHA page requesting keyboard shortcuts beyond clicking a checkbox or selecting images should be treated as malicious.

For organizations, Blackpoint researchers recommend monitoring for abuse of legitimate Windows components like SyncAppvPublishingServer.vbs, which attackers are now using to proxy PowerShell execution through trusted Microsoft binaries. Enterprise and education editions of Windows, which include the App-V virtualization framework, are particularly targeted.

The rapid proliferation of ClickFix builders — available on hacker forums for $200 to $1,500 per month — suggests the threat will continue to grow, according to The Hacker News. For tech professionals in the diaspora community working across enterprise environments, staying current on these evolving social engineering tactics is critical.
nri_angle: Many Indian diaspora professionals work in tech and enterprise environments targeted by these attacks — staying aware of ClickFix social engineering is critical for personal and organizational cybersecurity.
